---
title: "Efficient Words"
author: "DK"
date: "2026-06-20"
categories: [reflections, communications]
---

I recently wrote an email to a friend currently serving a mission in the Philippines.

We hadn’t seen each other in nearly two decades and had completely lost contact.

In a few paragraphs—a virtual "TL;DR"—I tried to pack in as much information as possible.

I explained why I had visited her hometown, shared a recent meeting with her brother (complete with a photo), recounted crossing paths with another friend from fifty years ago, and delivered a succinct update on my family.

It was a 534-word composition, written in a mix of Korean and English.

The opening paragraph of her reply was both a gentle assessment and an unexpected invitation:

> *"Your message was the shortest, most condensed, comprehensive writing I have ever read."*

She was reminding me, in a loving way, that something vital was missing.

I sounded like the prevailing voice of today. I had packed in the facts, but I had left out the feeling – An AI-like reporting.

![](images/20260528_165251.jpg)

---

This "report the facts" approach to communication is a habit I relied on throughout my childhood in Maryland and the first few years of my marriage.

Growing up, the dialogue between my immigrant parents and us children shrank over time, squeezed by a widening language gap and a lack of hours spent together.

Conversations with my sisters required very little participation from me.

By the time I entered college, the emotional depth of my communication was essentially stuck at a middle-school level.

When Sister K and I were celebrating our first wedding anniversary in Korea, we found ourselves physically separated.

She was in 대전, Daejeon with her family, and I was in 서울, Seoul with my uncle.

My uncle suggested I send her a 전보(電報)—a telegram.

Even well into the late twentieth century, long after most urgent news had shifted to the telephone, the telegram remained a formal, distinct way to send a message across the country via the post office.

Because telegrams charged by the character, economy of language was mandatory. The message we settled on was:

> **몸은 서울, 마음은 대전, 결혼 기념일을 자축 하면서...**
>
> *(Body in Seoul, heart in Daejeon, self-celebrating our wedding anniversary...)*

That 32-character message was the exact blueprint of my communication during the early stages of my marriage, and similar to how I spoke with my parents.

It was highly efficient, with a tiny hint of feeling added in, but entirely lacking the beautiful details of real life.

I didn’t describe the loneliness of spending time in Seoul by myself, the sights and sounds of the capital city, or the relatives I was visiting.

I had simply shared the 1990s equivalent of an AI summary.

![](images/20260615_163347.jpg)

---

I thought I had made progress in the decades since that first anniversary telegram.

Because I have read and responded to professional and personal emails since then, I figured my choice of words had become more refined, exact, and automatically deeper.

But judging by the reality check from the Philippines, I still have a long way to go.

When we rely on just the bare facts—the *who, what, when, and where*—the information moves from point A to point B.

The basic job gets done. But the thing that gets dropped in this efficiency mode is the *why*.

There is another hidden risk in just reporting the facts: it tricks us into thinking we are being completely objective.

In reality, we just end up trapped in our own narrow points of view.

We see things as we have been conditioned to see them, completely missing the bigger, higher intent—the heavenly view that sees what else is possible, through the opening of the other person's heart.

I don't know when or if AI will ever be advanced enough to understand and imitate human vulnerability or handle the fragile, emotional parts of a human conversations.

But instead of waiting for technology to solve a human problem, I know where I need to focus my energy.

I need to work on seeing things the way Sister K sees them.

I need to listen and discuss choices the way she understands them, and learn to make decisions and accept consequences alongside her.

In the end, I think that was the real intent of my friend’s letter.

It was a reminder to step out from behind the safe, analytical mindset of reporting.

It is time to bid farewell to efficiency, and to be, and show up, as a human being—messy, emotional, and fully present with the people that I love and admire.
